headline: Investors sold AI stocks and bought bonds Thursday, pulling the 10-year Treasury yield down 17bp to 4.96%, its first close under 5% in a month.
dateline: Friday, October 23, 2026 · closes as of Thu Oct 22

rundown.h: Traders all but wrote off a hike next week.
rundown.p: After Thursday's bond rally, futures put the odds of a quarter-point Fed hike on Oct 28 at just 10.5%. Pricing for the rest of the year still leans toward one more increase, with about a 22% chance of no further hike in 2026. For borrowers, the 2-year's 16bp drop to 4.65% is the cleanest read on how fast those expectations moved.

rundown.h: Chip stocks had their roughest day in months.
rundown.p: The PHLX Semiconductor Index fell more than 6% to 10,690, sitting just above its 200-day average, and the tech sector ETF lost 3.3% while consumer staples gained more than 3%. Lam Research's light guidance hit chip-equipment names. It's a sharp reversal from Wednesday's AI-hardware rally, and a reminder of how much of the market's gain rides on one theme.

rundown.h: Old-economy earnings mostly came in solid.
rundown.p: Texas Instruments posted $6.06 billion in sales and guided the fourth quarter to a $6.05 billion midpoint, above the $5.73 billion consensus. Honeywell beat on earnings and raised full-year guidance to $8.40–8.45 a share, Lockheed's backlog hit a record $292 billion, and Valero earned a record $23.90 a share. Intel reports next Thursday, Oct 29.

rundown.h: Builders are feeling 7% mortgages; Washington may step in.
rundown.p: PulteGroup's revenue of $3.97 billion missed the $4.15 billion expected as closings fell 9%. The administration is reportedly drafting an executive order on mortgage costs covering mortgage insurance, refinancing, and USDA and VA loans. Any relief would land in a market where the 30-year rate is still above 7%, and housing stocks rallied Thursday as yields fell.

rundown.h: Investors are bailing on single stocks at a record pace.
rundown.p: Bank of America said its clients pulled a record net $14.8 billion from individual stocks, while Goldman Sachs said hedge funds' short leverage is in the 99th percentile of the past five years. Heavy short positioning can fuel sharp rebounds, but together the flows show professionals and individuals alike growing more defensive with indexes near records.

rundown.h: Layoffs still aren't showing up in the claims data.
rundown.p: Initial jobless claims fell to 194,000 last week, below the 200,000 expected, and the four-week average eased to 197,750. Continuing claims rose to 1.728 million from 1.703 million, a sign that people who lose jobs are taking longer to find new ones. A firm job market gives the Fed less reason to rush toward cuts.

dive.title: Apartments are now the problem child in CMBS
dive.dek: CMBS delinquency hit its highest level since 2020 in September, and the newest pressure is coming from multifamily, not office.
dive.body:
For three years the commercial mortgage story was about office towers. September's numbers say the stress has spread. Trepp's overall CMBS delinquency rate rose to 8.02% from 7.85% in August, the highest since late 2020. Office is still the worst sector at 12.16%, but it's just below January's record 12.34%. The sharper move came from apartments: multifamily delinquency jumped 35bp in a month to 8.04%, up from 6.59% a year earlier and now above the overall rate.

Special servicing, where troubled loans go to be worked out, tells the same story. Trepp's special servicing rate reached 11.49% in September, the highest since February 2013 and up 84bp from a year earlier. New transfers totaled $2.65 billion across 42 loans, 57% of it office, led by One SoHo Square ($512.8 million) and a Starwood regional mall portfolio ($436.9 million). Trepp said five large single-asset, single-borrower loans drove much of the delinquency increase. Industrial remains the clean corner at 1.14%, though that's double the 0.56% of a year ago.

The spread beyond office matters because apartments have long been treated as the safe corner of commercial real estate. Lodging delinquency also rose, by 34bp to 6.18%. Retail, at 6.58%, was the only major sector that improved over the year.

There is one hopeful sign: resolutions, meaning payoffs, modifications and liquidations, rose 237% in September to $1.95 billion from $579.7 million in August. KBRA, which tracks its own rated deals, puts its distress rate at 10.3%, down 31bp from a year earlier even as its conduit distress rate rose. If resolutions stay high and rates keep easing, the pipeline drains. If floating-rate apartment loans keep defaulting, lenders will tighten terms across property types, including industrial.

items.title: October Philly Fed: activity cooled to 20.9, but factories raised their own prices faster
items.body:
The Philadelphia Fed's manufacturing index fell to 20.9 in October from 37.8, short of the 28.4 consensus and the slowest expansion since June. New orders dropped to 4.3 from 29.2, shipments to 15.3 from 27.7 and unfilled orders to 2.4 from 20.4. Employment slipped to 9.1 and the workweek to 7.5, its lowest since June.

On prices, the input gauge eased to 43.2 from 48.6, with more than 43% of firms reporting higher costs and none reporting lower ones. The prices-received index rose to 40.1 from 31.3, its highest since May 2025, and more than 41% of firms said they raised their own prices. Over the past two years prices paid has ranged from 28.1 (Nov 2024) to 64.3 (Aug 2025).

Six-month expectations cooled: future activity fell to 33.0, the lowest since January, while future prices paid (62.9) and received (62.1) stayed well above long-run averages. The 10-year yield fell and the curve flattened on the day, despite a hotter-than-expected PPI released at the same time.

experts.view: The report shows a clear slowdown in factory activity even though the index is still positive, and markets appear to be starting to worry about growth.

lead.title: Washington talks of a long war as Iran claims new tanker hits
lead.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said Thursday it struck four vessels using the U.S.-endorsed southern route through the Gulf and that three more hit mines, then claimed Friday it had disabled seven tankers near Hormuz. None of the claims had been independently confirmed, but the UAE reported an oil spill from a tanker on Oct 23 and closed beaches in Umm Al Quwain. U.S. UN Ambassador Mike Waltz told the Financial Times the war could last another year and that the Navy can hold its blockade of Iranian ports indefinitely.

On the Saudi side, Aramco ordered staff out of its Dhahran headquarters after this week's drone attacks. CEO Amin Nasser said flows on the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which bypasses Hormuz, have risen to 7 million barrels a day from 2 million. European and regional foreign ministers met in Istanbul Friday; a UK statement said Hormuz traffic remains sharply below pre-war levels.
lead.reach: Through oil and fuel costs. Brent settled up 4% at $113.17 on Oct 22, its highest since May 18, and traded near $114 early Oct 23; renewed strike threats after the Nov 3 midterms keep the risk premium in place.

reading.title: Bogle's Folly: the fund nobody wanted
reading.dek: In 1976 Jack Bogle launched the first index mutual fund to a chorus of skeptics, and proved that keeping costs low is the surest edge in investing.
body: On August 31, 1976, a fund almost nobody seemed to want opened for business. John C. Bogle, who had spent roughly two decades rising through Wellington Management before being ousted over a merger he later regretted, was betting on a radical idea: instead of paying managers to pick winners, simply own the whole S&P 500 and charge as little as possible. He called it the First Index Investment Trust. Skeptics had a less flattering name for it: Bogle's Folly.

The roots went back to 1951, when Bogle's Princeton thesis, The Economic Role of the Investment Company, identified costs as a drag on fund performance. A quarter-century later he finally had a vehicle to act on that insight. His newly formed Vanguard Group had an unusual design: the company is owned by the funds it runs, and therefore by their shareholders, so there was no outside owner demanding a slice of the fees. Even so, Wellington's board still had to approve the index fund before it could launch.

The launch was a flop. Bogle hoped the underwriting would bring in $50 million to $150 million; it raised a little more than $11 million, a result he himself described in the bluntest terms. The banks handling the offering suggested scrapping the fund altogether. Bogle refused. His logic was plain arithmetic: investors as a group earn the market's return before costs, so a low-fee fund that owns the entire market should, over long stretches, finish ahead of most investors paying for active management.

Time proved him right, though slowly; the advantage built through patient compounding rather than any single dazzling year. The fund, now called the Vanguard 500 Index Fund, started with annual operating expenses of 0.43%; today its Admiral Shares charge 0.04% and its ETF shares 0.03%. Vanguard grew into a giant with roughly $13.3 trillion in global assets as of 2025, and indexing went from punchline to the default choice for millions of savers. Bogle, who died in 2019 at 89, spent his later years preaching the same message in books such as The Little Book of Common Sense Investing.

The enduring lesson is that costs are the one part of investing you fully control. Returns are uncertain; fees are guaranteed. A percentage point a year sounds trivial, but compounded over decades it can eat a large share of an investor's ending wealth. Bogle never promised to beat the market. He promised to stop losing to the middlemen, and that turned out to be enough.

quote.src: John Bogle, on the fund's 1976 offering (via Vanguard)
